transcript:
Meeting header: 2025-10-28 10:30 UTC | Duration 65m | Attendees: Evan (Redwood AE), Sam (Redwood SE), Priya (CSM); Dr. Lina, Raj, Tanya, Noah (Miramar)

Summary: Quick quality gate/weekly check on the 3-week POC — focus on prompt set fidelity, scoring drift observed in last batch, and guardrail false positives. Agree next steps for regression sweep and security followups.

[00:00] Evan: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. Quick note, we'll try to keep this tight — got about an hour. The main things on our side are the regression results we ran on Tuesday and a couple of guardrail tuning experiments Sam wanted to walk through.
[00:18] Dr. Lina: Thanks. We have 2 med directors on the call today but I'll be the voice. We've seen some odd outputs in triage summaries — some hallucinations and a few safety flags on benign clinical language.
[00:31] Raj: Yeah, I'll upload the exact examples after this call. A lot are short context prompts that mention "prior episodes" and the model invents meds.
[00:40] Sam: Right, that matches what we saw. The regression run (v1.2 -> v1.3) showed a 4.2% drop in accuracy on the short-note prompt set, but steady precision on longer context. We suspect prompt truncation + KV cache boundary behavior.
[00:58] Tanya: Can you explain KV cache boundary? I'm not sure I follow the technical detail.
[01:05] Sam: Sure — when the model is serving many requests, the runtime uses a key-value cache per session to avoid recomputing previous tokens. If the request boundary splits a clinical note mid-sentence the cached context tokens aren't aligned with the scoring prompt template and you can get plausible-sounding but incorrect completions. It's subtle and shows up more on shorter prompts.
[01:28] Dr. Lina: Okay makes sense. So is that a Redwood runtime thing or the model?
[01:33] Evan: It's more of an interaction — runtime + prompt engineering. We've seen this before on other customers; there are two mitigations: prefix normalization (we add a sentinel and re-tokenize) and prompt-level padding so the KV cache boundaries are consistent. Both are config changes on the serving side.
[01:51] Raj: Padding sounds safe, but will that impact latency? Our SLO is p95 < 300ms.
[01:56] Sam: Small increase on cold sessions, but for ongoing sessions it's negligible. We can run the patch in a canary pool and measure p95 — that's in the next steps.

[02:15] Evan: Quick pivot — guardrails. We saw a batch where the safety filter flagged 37 examples from the test set; after manual review only 9 were actual violations. So 28 false positives.
[02:27] Dr. Lina: Those 28 were problematic because they blocked clinical summaries from passing QA. We need fewer false positives — the clinicians are losing trust.
[02:34] Sam: Agreed. The safety model is tuned to be conservative. We have two levers: 1) relax the threshold, 2) add a secondary whitelist / allowlist for known-safe clinical tokens and patterns. Relaxing threshold reduces recall for truly problematic cases, so we lean toward a pattern-based whitelist plus post-classifier heuristics.
[02:53] Noah: From security's perspective, whitelists make me nervous — do you have audit trails for overrides? We require an immutable log for any suppressed safety hit.
[03:02] Evan: Yes, Redwood Console will log the original decision, the rule that triggered the override, the operator, and a checksum. That log is in the audit table and exportable. We'll share a sample CSV.

[03:20] Raj: On scoring — you mentioned the rubric. What metrics are you using for the short-note set? We currently track a binary correctness label and an annotator confidence score.
[03:29] Sam: For the POC we use a composite score: factuality (0-1), actionability (0-1), and hallucination penalty (0-1). The overall quality score is weighted: 0.5 factuality + 0.3 actionability + 0.2 (1 - hallucination). For short notes the factuality variance increased which drove down the overall.
[03:52] Dr. Lina: Can you share an example where the model's summary got the medication wrong?
[03:57] Raj: I have one here — prompt: "Patient A, prior EtOH abuse, admitted 2/3 for GI bleed. Current meds: none listed." Model output asserted "Started on metoprolol" — totally fabricated.
[04:10] Sam: That's a classic hallucination when the model attempts to fill structured slots. We're introducing a placeholder token and forcing the model to respond with a JSON schema for the meds field, plus using a stricter decoder sampling (greedy/top-k small) for these slots.
[04:29] Tanya: Will that change our latency or token costs significantly?
[04:34] Sam: Slightly more tokens for the JSON wrapper, but overall token delta small; cost increase ~2-3% on these workflows but precision improves a lot. We'll quantify in the regression.

[04:55] Evan: On the regression results we ran — quick bullets: overall BLEU/ROUGE aren't great proxies for this domain; we used token-level factual overlap (TP/FP/FN), and a human-agreed label set of 1,200 examples. Most drift concentrated in prompts under 80 tokens.
[05:16] Dr. Lina: Does the human label set include edge clinical cases like multi-morbidity?
[05:20] Sam: Yes, deliberately oversampled complex cases. We'll share the sampling stratification.
[05:26] Raj: One ask — can Redwood produce a per-prompt debug trace showing token logits or top-5 next-word candidates? That would help us triage systematically.
[05:36] Sam: We can capture a per-request debug trace in canary mode — it'll include top-k logits for up to the final 64 tokens. Note: sensitive data masking is on by default in logs; raw PHI isn't persisted.
[05:51] Noah: Confirm masking? We need to know if any PHI leaves the VPC for hosted runs.
[05:56] Evan: For the Dedicated and Private offerings, customer data stays in your VPC. For hosted we have optional ingestion filters; by default we redact common PHI patterns in the pipeline and store only hashed artifacts for debug traces. We'll send the security doc that explains the retention and masking pipeline.

[06:18] Tanya: Back to guardrails — the whitelist approach sounds promising. What about rare cases where the whitelist blocks a real issue?
[06:26] Sam: Good point. We'll implement whitelist rules with confidence thresholds and a fallback to full classifier if pattern matched but confidence low. That preserves recall while reducing false positives.

[06:40] Evan: Let's go through concrete next steps and owners: first, Redwood will run a regression sweep on 2,000 seed prompts including the short-note oversample and produce CSVs with per-prompt scores + top-3 failure reason tags. Second, we'll spin up a canary to test the KV-cache padding and JSON-slot enforcement for meds. Third, Sam will run a guardrail FPR analysis and generate whitelist candidate patterns.
[07:05] Raj: We'll provide the 20 flagged examples and current prod prompt config within 48 hours.
[07:10] Dr. Lina: We also need a lightweight clinician-facing checklist for when a safety flag is suppressed — to ensure QA continuity.
[07:18] Priya: Redwood CSMs can draft a checklist template and share it for approval — that's reasonable.

[07:30] Evan: Timeline: regression CSV by 2025-11-03, whitelist candidate set by 2025-11-05, canary perf run week of 2025-11-10. Security docs and SOC2 artifacts shared by 2025-11-07.

[07:45] Tanya: One more question on eval metrics: can we add annotator confidence into the scoring pipeline and weight low-confidence labels less?
[07:52] Sam: Yes, we can implement weighted scoring so labels with low annotator confidence contribute less to the aggregate. That helps smooth variance. We'll include that in the regression script.

[08:05] Evan: Anything else?
[08:08] Noah: Can you confirm the audit log format (CSV columns)? I want event_ts, request_id, decision, override_rule, operator, checksum.
[08:15] Evan: Yep, that's the format — we'll attach a sample export.

[08:25] Dr. Lina: Appreciate the quick turnaround. If we can get the false positives down and the hallucination slots tightened, the clinicians will be okay moving to a partial pilot.
[08:33] Evan: Great — we'll follow up with the artifacts and schedule the bench. Thanks everyone.

Closeout: Meeting ended 11:35 UTC.

References and shared artifacts: "regression-results-week3.csv" (Redwood internal link), "miramar-flagged-examples.zip" (customer upload), "security-overview-S4.pdf" (Redwood shared link).

Notes on transcription: occasional mis-hears on acronyms (KV cache transcribed sometimes as "K V C") and names (Rajesh sometimes appears as "Raj"). Some crosstalk at ~07:10 when Priya and Dr. Lina overlap.
